client: I just missed the deadline for my final university project, and I can't stop worrying about how badly this is going to affect my grade. I keep playing all these worst-case scenarios in my head - like maybe I'll fail the class or it'll ruin my GPA. It's making it hard to focus on anything else, even though logically I know one assignment isn't everything.
therapist: It sounds like you're really caught in a cycle of anxious thoughts about this missed deadline. I notice your voice sounds even more distressed than your words suggest - would you say you're feeling even more upset about this than you're letting on? Let's examine these worst-case scenarios together - what evidence do you have that this one assignment will completely derail your academic progress?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I am more upset than I’m letting on. It’s just that this isn’t just about one assignment—it feels like it’s proof that I’m not good enough or capable enough to handle everything. I keep thinking about how my professor will see me as unreliable, and that could ruin my chances for recommendations later. It’s hard to believe this won’t completely derail me.
therapist: I hear how deeply this situation is affecting your sense of self-worth. You're connecting this one event to bigger fears about your capabilities - would it be helpful to look at whether there's a pattern of unreliability, or if this is more about the meaning you're giving to a single setback?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess I do tend to make small mistakes into big proof that I'm not good enough. But it's hard not to - when I mess up at work, it feels like confirmation of all my worst fears. Like if I can't even handle this simple task right, how can I trust myself with anything important? 

The idea that this might just be one setback and not a pattern is... well, it's hard to believe. My brain immediately jumps to all the other times I've felt inadequate.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing a pattern where mistakes trigger strong feelings of self-doubt. When you say it's hard to believe this might just be one setback, I wonder if we could explore how these thoughts might be affecting you differently now than they did in past situations? What makes this particular moment feel so definitive?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know logically that setbacks happen to everyone, but this one feels heavier because it was in front of my whole team at work. Now I keep replaying their reactions in my head and imagining they've lost respect for me. It's like my brain keeps telling me this mistake defines my whole capability.
therapist: I hear how much this public mistake is weighing on you - it's understandable to feel exposed when something goes wrong in front of colleagues. You mentioned replaying their reactions - have you considered that what you're imagining they're thinking might be more about your own self-judgment than their actual perceptions?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, but I actually saw their faces when it happened - the awkward smiles and quick glances away. It's not just in my head. I keep thinking they must see me as incompetent now, and that makes me avoid team meetings because I don't want to face them.
therapist: It sounds like those nonverbal reactions from your colleagues really stuck with you. I notice you're describing avoiding team meetings now - how do you think this avoidance might be affecting both your work relationships and your own confidence in the long run?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know avoiding meetings isn't great, but every time I go I just end up obsessing over people's facial expressions afterward. It's like I can't focus on the actual work because I'm so worried they're judging me or think I'm incompetent. The more I avoid, the more awkward I feel when I do have to interact with them.
therapist: I hear how exhausting this cycle of worrying about others' perceptions has become for you. You're stuck between avoiding interactions and then feeling even more anxious when they happen - could we explore what it would look like to shift your focus from reading faces to engaging with the actual content of the meetings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it's not that simple for me. When I'm in meetings, my brain just automatically scans everyone's expressions for disapproval, and I can't seem to stop it. Even if I try to focus on the content, I keep getting distracted by wondering if someone's frown means they think my idea is stupid.
therapist: It sounds like this hyper-vigilance for disapproval has become almost automatic for you in meetings. I notice you're describing this as something that happens to you rather than something you choose - would it be helpful to explore small ways you might begin to redirect that attention when you notice it happening?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about redirecting my attention, but it's not that simple. When I'm in a meeting and someone frowns or checks their phone, my stomach just drops automatically - like my body reacts before I can even think. 

And honestly, the idea of choosing where to focus my attention sounds exhausting. I already feel like I'm working so hard just to hold it together in those situations.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming and automatic these physical reactions feel for you in meetings - it sounds like your body is carrying a lot of this anxiety even before your mind can catch up. When you mention feeling exhausted from trying to hold it together, I wonder if we could explore what it might look like to approach these situations with slightly less pressure on yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about less pressure, but in meetings I feel like I *have* to keep it together. If I let my guard down even a little, I'm terrified people will notice my shaking hands or hear my voice cracking. The exhaustion comes from constantly monitoring myself like that. 

It's not that simple to just relax when my promotion depends on appearing competent. What if trying to be less perfect makes me look worse?
therapist: You're describing such an intense pressure to maintain this image of perfection in meetings - it sounds like you're carrying both the exhaustion of constant self-monitoring and the fear of what might happen if you let your guard down. What would it feel like to imagine that your colleagues might be more understanding of your humanity than you're allowing yourself to believe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... I get what you're saying, but it's hard to imagine them being understanding. Last week when Sarah stumbled over her words in a presentation, people were whispering and rolling their eyes afterward. That's exactly what I'm terrified of happening to me. 

The pressure feels so real because I've seen how judgmental people can be. Maybe they'd be more forgiving with someone else, but I feel like I've set this standard for myself where any mistake would be catastrophic.
therapist: I hear how observing that reaction to Sarah has reinforced your fears about making mistakes in front of others. You're holding onto this belief that you've set an impossibly high standard for yourself - what do you think might happen if you allowed yourself the same margin for error that you might extend to a colleague?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
